topic: Substitutes, oils and the refrigeration system

notes.front: Under the Section 608 rules, what does it mean to retrofit an appliance?
notes.back: To convert an appliance from one refrigerant to another refrigerant.
notes.explanation: The definition covers the whole conversion, not only the change of fluid: it includes making the system compatible with the new refrigerant.
notes.example: Converting a cold room to run on a different refrigerant is a retrofit; adding more of the same refrigerant to it is not.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions
notes.evidence: Retrofit means to convert an appliance from one refrigerant to another refrigerant. Retrofitting includes the conversion of the appliance to achieve system compatibility with the new refrigerant
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a “drop-in” replacement refrigerant, and do the Section 608 test topics say one exists?
notes.back: A substitute that could go into existing equipment with no other change. The test topics list the absence of drop-in replacements.
notes.explanation: The test topics do not define the term; the gloss is the plain meaning of the words. The item sits under substitute refrigerants and oils, next to the incompatibility of substitutes with many older lubricants.
notes.example: Like a spare part sold as fitting every model with no changes: the test topics say refrigerants offer no such part.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Absence of "drop-in" replacements - Incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with CFC and HCFC refrigerants

notes.front: In the Section 608 test topics, what kind of product is an ester?
notes.back: A lubricant: one of the lubricant types a technician should be able to match to a given refrigerant.
notes.explanation: The test topics name esters as an example when they ask technicians to identify the lubricants for given refrigerants.
notes.example: Like one grade of oil among several, each suited to particular machines rather than to all of them.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: identification of lubricants for given refrigerants, such as esters with R-134

notes.front: In the Section 608 test topics, what kind of product is an alkylbenzene?
notes.back: A lubricant: the second example the test topics give of matching a lubricant to particular refrigerants.
notes.explanation: The test topics list alkylbenzenes right after esters, in the same item on identifying lubricants for given refrigerants.
notes.example: Like a second grade of oil on the workshop shelf, kept for a different family of machines from the first.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: identification of lubricants for given refrigerants, such as esters with R-134; alkylbenzenes for HCFCs

notes.front: What is fractionation in a refrigerant blend?
notes.back: The tendency of the different components of a blend to leak at different rates.
notes.explanation: The test topics call it the fractionation problem and list it among the issues with substitute refrigerants and oils.
notes.example: Like a torn bag of mixed rice and flour: the flour escapes faster, so what remains is no longer the mix you started with.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Fractionation problem--tendency of different components of blends to leak at different rates

notes.front: What are two changes the rule says a retrofit may include?
notes.back: For example, changes in lubricants and gaskets. Filters, driers, valves, o-rings and appliance components are also listed.
notes.explanation: The rule’s list is open (“not limited to”): it covers what the conversion needs to reach system compatibility with the new refrigerant.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions
notes.evidence: Retrofitting includes the conversion of the appliance to achieve system compatibility with the new refrigerant and may include, but is not limited to, changes in lubricants, gaskets, filters, driers, valves, o-rings or appliance components.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: The Section 608 test topics list the {{c1::absence}} of “drop-in” replacement refrigerants.
notes.back: absence
notes.explanation: The item is followed at once by the incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with the older refrigerants.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Absence of "drop-in" replacements - Incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with CFC and HCFC refrigerants

notes.front: According to the test topics, how do substitute refrigerants get on with the lubricants used with chlorofluorocarbon and hydrochlorofluorocarbon refrigerants?
notes.back: Badly, in many cases: substitutes are incompatible with many of those lubricants.
notes.explanation: The hedge is “many”, not “all”: the oil already in an older system cannot simply be assumed to suit a substitute.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with CFC and HCFC refrigerants

notes.front: Does lubricant incompatibility run only one way, from substitutes to the older lubricants?
notes.back: No. Chlorofluorocarbon and hydrochlorofluorocarbon refrigerants are also incompatible with many new lubricants.
notes.explanation: The test topics state both directions in one item, so neither pairing of old and new can be taken for granted.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with CFC and HCFC refrigerants and incompatibility of CFC and HCFC refrigerants with many new lubricants

notes.front: The test topics give {{c1::esters}} as the lubricants to identify with R-134.
notes.back: esters
notes.explanation: This is one of two examples the test topics give of matching lubricants to given refrigerants.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: identification of lubricants for given refrigerants, such as esters with R-134

notes.front: The test topics pair {{c1::alkylbenzene}} lubricants with hydrochlorofluorocarbon refrigerants.
notes.back: alkylbenzene
notes.explanation: It is the second example in the same item, after esters for R-134.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: identification of lubricants for given refrigerants, such as esters with R-134; alkylbenzenes for HCFCs

notes.front: Which refrigerants can suffer from fractionation, according to the test topics?
notes.back: Blends: refrigerants made of more than one component.
notes.explanation: Fractionation is about different components leaking at different rates, and only a blend has different components.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Fractionation problem--tendency of different components of blends to leak at different rates

notes.front: A technician plans to charge a substitute refrigerant into a system that ran on a hydrochlorofluorocarbon, keeping the existing oil. What do the test topics warn about?
notes.back: Many substitutes are incompatible with the lubricants used with the older refrigerants.
notes.choices:
A) Many substitutes are incompatible with lubricants used with the older refrigerants
B) Nothing: any lubricant works with any refrigerant
C) Only that the new refrigerant must be a blend
notes.choicesExplained: B: the test topics list incompatibility in both directions, so lubricants are not interchangeable. C: nothing in the item requires a blend; blends raise a different problem, fractionation.
notes.explanation: The existing oil is a lubricant used with a hydrochlorofluorocarbon, and the test topics say substitutes are incompatible with many such lubricants.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with CFC and HCFC refrigerants

notes.front: A supplier sells a refrigerant as a “drop-in” for older equipment, needing no other change. How should a technician weigh the claim, going by the test topics?
notes.back: With caution: the test topics list the absence of drop-in replacements.
notes.choices:
A) With caution, since the test topics list the absence of drop-in replacements
B) As proof that the lubricant can stay as it is
C) As a legal requirement to switch refrigerants
notes.choicesExplained: B: the test topics warn that substitutes are incompatible with many older lubricants. C: a sales description creates no legal duty.
notes.explanation: The test topics list the absence of drop-in replacements right beside the incompatibility of substitutes with many older lubricants.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Absence of "drop-in" replacements - Incompatibility of substitute refrigerants with many lubricants used with CFC and HCFC refrigerants

notes.front: A system runs on R-134. Which lubricant type do the test topics associate with it: ester or alkylbenzene?
notes.back: Ester.
notes.explanation: The test topics pair esters with R-134 and keep alkylbenzenes for the hydrochlorofluorocarbons.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: identification of lubricants for given refrigerants, such as esters with R-134; alkylbenzenes for HCFCs

notes.front: A system runs on a hydrochlorofluorocarbon refrigerant. Which lubricant type do the test topics associate with it: ester or alkylbenzene?
notes.back: Alkylbenzene.
notes.explanation: The test topics pair alkylbenzenes with hydrochlorofluorocarbons, and esters with R-134.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: identification of lubricants for given refrigerants, such as esters with R-134; alkylbenzenes for HCFCs

notes.front: A system charged with a refrigerant blend has had a slow leak. Which problem from the test topics should the technician keep in mind?
notes.back: Fractionation: the blend’s components may have leaked at different rates.
notes.choices:
A) Fractionation
B) The absence of drop-in replacements
C) Alkylbenzene lubricant
notes.choicesExplained: B: that item concerns replacing one refrigerant with another, not a leak. C: alkylbenzene is a lubricant type, not a leak problem.
notes.explanation: Fractionation is defined by components leaking at different rates, so a leak from a blend is exactly where it arises.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Substitute Refrigerants and oils”
notes.evidence: Fractionation problem--tendency of different components of blends to leak at different rates

notes.front: An owner converts an R-22 system to a different refrigerant, changing its lubricant and gaskets to suit. What does the rule call this?
notes.back: A retrofit.
notes.explanation: Converting an appliance from one refrigerant to another is a retrofit, and the rule says the conversion may include lubricant and gasket changes.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions
notes.evidence: Retrofitting includes the conversion of the appliance to achieve system compatibility with the new refrigerant and may include, but is not limited to, changes in lubricants, gaskets, filters, driers, valves, o-rings or appliance components.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What are two methods the rule gives for finding where an appliance is leaking refrigerant?
notes.back: For example, ultrasonic tests and gas-imaging cameras. Bubble tests and leak detection devices are also listed.
notes.explanation: The rule’s list is open: it says the potential methods include, but are not limited to, these.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions (“Leak inspection”)
notes.evidence: Potential methods include, but are not limited to, ultrasonic tests, gas-imaging cameras, bubble tests as appropriate, or the use of a leak detection device operated and maintained according to manufacturer guidelines.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under the rule, may a method that shows only that an appliance is leaking be used on its own to look for leaks?
notes.back: No. It must be used together with a method that can find where the leak is.
notes.explanation: Such methods tell you refrigerant is escaping but, as the rule puts it, not the location of the leak.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions (“Leak inspection”)
notes.evidence: Methods that determine whether the appliance is leaking refrigerant but not the location of a leak, such as standing pressure/vacuum decay tests, sight glass checks, viewing receiver levels, pressure checks, and charging charts, must be used in conjunction with methods that can determine the location of a leak.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What are two methods the rule lists for checking a leak repair once the appliance is back to normal operation?
notes.back: For example, soap bubbles and electronic or ultrasonic leak detectors. Pressure or vacuum tests and infrared tests are also listed.
notes.explanation: The rule’s list is open (“not limited to”), and soap bubbles are qualified with “as appropriate”.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions (“Follow-up verification test”)
notes.evidence: Potential methods for follow-up verification tests include, but are not limited to, the use of soap bubbles as appropriate, electronic or ultrasonic leak detectors, pressure or vacuum tests, fluorescent dye and black light, infrared or near infrared tests, and handheld gas detection devices.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What separates the two groups of leak-checking methods the rule describes?
notes.back: One group finds where a leak is; the other shows only that the appliance is leaking and must be paired with the first.
notes.explanation: Decay tests, sight glass checks, pressure checks and charging charts reveal a leak but not its location, so the rule adds a locating method.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions (“Leak inspection”)
